topic: Why f-stops go 1.4, 2, 2.8, 4: f-number is a ratio, light follows area, each stop is x sqrt(2)
lines: Why do f-stops go one point four, two, two point eight, four...
instead of just one, two, three, four?
Because an f-number isn't a size. It's a ratio.
Focal length, divided by the width of the opening.
A fifty millimeter lens at f two has a hole twenty-five millimeters wide.
A 50mm lens at f/2 has a hole 25mm wide.
But light doesn't care about width. It cares about area.
Make the hole twice as wide, and four times the light gets in.
Photographers wanted every step to cut the light exactly in half.
Half the area means the width shrinks by the square root of two.
Multiply again and again: one point four, two, two point eight, four, five point six, eight, eleven, sixteen.
Every click is half the light. From f one point four to f sixteen, that's a hundred and twenty-eight times less.
Every click is half the light. From f/1.4 to f/16, that's 128 times less.
It was never random. It's the square root of two, hiding on every lens.

youtube.title: Why F-Stops Go 1.4, 2, 2.8, 4 (Not 1, 2, 3, 4)
youtube.description:
The f-number is a ratio: focal length ÷ aperture diameter (a 50mm lens at f/2 has a 25mm opening). Light depends on the AREA of the opening, and area grows with the square of the width. To halve the light each stop, the width must shrink by √2 ≈ 1.414 — so the f-numbers multiply by √2: 1.4, 2, 2.8, 4, 5.6, 8, 11, 16 (rounded). f/1.4 → f/16 is 7 stops = 2^7 = 128× less light.
